title: Clafoutis
subtitle: Limousin baked cherry custard
excerpt: Whole cherries baked in a light egg and milk batter until puffed, golden, and just set. A regional speciality of the Limousin in central France, made from the black cherries of the region. Simple to prepare and served warm from the dish.
sourceNotes: Clafoutis is the regional dessert of the Limousin (Corrèze, Creuse, Haute-Vienne). The name comes from the Occitan 'clafir', meaning to fill or to stuff. The cherries of the Limousin, particularly the Guigne de Sainte-Lucie, are the traditional fruit. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives the recipe with the note that the cherries are left unpitted: the stones impart a faint almond flavour from the kernels during baking. Elizabeth David includes it in French Provincial Cooking (1960). Versions made with other stone fruit (plums, apricots, pears) are technically called flaugnarde in France, though the term clafoutis is now used colloquially for any fruit version.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best served warm, 10 to 20 minutes out of the oven. Can be served at room temperature the same day but will deflate as it cools, as all egg-set batters do. Does not keep well overnight.

glossaryTerms.definition: A mixture of flour, eggs, and liquid (milk or cream) thin enough to pour. Clafoutis batter is similar to a crêpe batter but slightly richer, and baked rather than fried. The eggs set during baking, giving the clafoutis its characteristic custardy texture around the fruit.

content.text: Clafoutis is one of the quickest French desserts to prepare. A simple

of eggs, flour, sugar, and milk is poured over cherries in a buttered dish and baked until puffed and golden. It looks impressive and requires almost no skill: measuring, whisking, and pouring are the extent of the technique. The result is somewhere between a thick crêpe and a light baked custard, with the cherries providing a slight sourness and juice that cuts through the richness.

The authentic Limousin version leaves the cherries unpitted. The stones release a faint almond flavour as the clafoutis bakes. Many cooks prefer to pit them for ease of eating; either approach is correct.

items.prepNote: fresh, stalks removed; pitted or unpitted (see above)

content.text: Heat the oven to 180°C fan. Butter the gratin dish generously and dust with caster sugar, tapping out the excess. Spread the cherries in a single layer across the base of the dish.

Whisk the eggs and sugar together until the sugar has dissolved and the mixture is pale. Add the flour and whisk until smooth. Gradually pour in the milk and cream, whisking constantly to produce a smooth, pourable batter. Add the vanilla extract.

Pour the batter over the cherries. Transfer to the oven and bake for 35 to 40 minutes until the clafoutis is puffed and golden at the edges and the centre is just set with a very slight wobble. A skewer inserted into the batter (not a cherry) should come out with moist, not wet, crumbs.
Allow to rest for 10 minutes, it will sink slightly as it cools. Dust generously with icing sugar and serve warm, directly from the dish.

items.symptom: The clafoutis is liquid in the centre after 40 minutes
items.cause: The oven was not properly preheated, or the dish was too deep relative to its surface area.
items.fix: Continue baking in 5-minute increments. A large, shallow gratin dish bakes faster and more evenly than a deep one. The centre will firm as it cools even if it appears very soft when taken from the oven.

items.cause: The flour was added all at once and not whisked in before the liquid.
items.fix: Always whisk the flour into the egg and sugar mixture before adding the milk. Adding liquid to flour that has not been incorporated into the eggs first causes lumping. Pass through a fine sieve if lumps remain before pouring over the cherries.

items.symptom: The clafoutis has sunk completely flat
items.cause: It was left to cool for too long before serving.
items.fix: A clafoutis will always deflate as it cools, this is normal. It should be served warm, within 20 minutes of coming out of the oven. A flat, cooled clafoutis still tastes good but lacks the dramatic puffed look of a freshly baked one.

content.text: The Limousin in central France is black cherry country. The Guigne de Sainte-Lucie and the Bigarreau grow there, and the clafoutis is built around them. It is still made in farmhouses across the Corrèze and Creuse each June and July. The name appears in cookbooks from the mid-19th century, but the dish is older. Outside France, it has been widely adopted: simple to make, easy to describe, and very good.
